scoutNotes: The PR moves interest accrual from a once-a-day operator cron into an hourly in-process timer on the server, guarding re-crediting with a new per-account `lastAccruedOn` day marker (migration 004, additive) so the job can run more than once a day safely. It removes the README's "not safe to run twice" caveat and adds a test that calls `accrueInterest` twice with a pinned clock to show only one credit lands.

confirmed.title: Local-vs-UTC day mismatch double-credits interest
confirmed.rootCause: accrueInterest compares a locally-formatted 'today' (dayOf via toLocaleDateString with no timeZone) against lastAccruedOn stored as the UTC calendar day (at.slice(0,10)), so the 'already credited today' guard mismatches for hours each day on non-UTC hosts and re-credits interest — and the new test only pins the clock to noon UTC, far from the mismatch window, so it cannot catch this.
confirmed.summary: The skip check compares a UTC-derived stored day against a locally-formatted 'today', so on any server not running in the UTC timezone the hourly job re-credits interest instead of skipping already-credited accounts.
confirmed.failure: On a server not running in UTC (e.g. TZ=Asia/Kolkata, UTC+5:30), during the hours each day when the local calendar day has rolled over but the UTC day has not, every hourly accrueInterest tick computes dayOf(clock()) as the new local day while the account's lastAccruedOn still holds the previous UTC day, so the 'already credited today' check never matches and the account is credited again on the next hourly tick within that window, duplicating interest.

sites.title: Local-day vs UTC-day mismatch double-credits interest
lastAccruedOn stored in UTC, compared in local time
Test pins noon UTC, hides TZ day-mismatch bug

confirmed.reasoning: Reproduced directly: with TZ=Asia/Kolkata, accrueInterest called at 2026-03-02T20:00:00Z then 2026-03-02T21:00:00Z (same UTC calendar day) credited interest twice (balance went 100000 -> 100013 -> 100026), because dayOf() (src/interest.js:16) uses toLocaleDateString('en-CA') with no timeZone option (host-local day), while lastAccruedOn is persisted as at.slice(0,10) (src/interest.js:35), the UTC day from toISOString(). These diverge for several hours a day on any non-UTC host. Confirmed via git show that dayOf, the skip check, and migration 004 are all newly introduced in this commit, and that src/server.js now wires accrueInterest(store) into a setInterval(...) using the default system clock, so this reaches production on any non-UTC host. Also confirmed the new test in test/interest.test.js pins both calls to 12:00:00.000Z, 24 hours apart, which stays outside the mismatch window for realistic timezone offsets, so it does not catch the bug.
confirmed.panel: 3 of 3 skeptics could not refute it

confirmed.title: Hourly job blocks event loop under load
confirmed.rootCause: The hourly interest job now runs its synchronous, unbatched loop over all accounts directly inside the HTTP server's event loop, blocking all concurrent request handling for the duration of the job.
confirmed.summary: The setInterval callback runs accrueInterest's single-threaded, unbatched for-loop over all accounts synchronously inside the HTTP server's event loop, with no bound on how long that can take, so every concurrent request stalls for the job's full duration once an hour.
confirmed.failure: With N accounts in the store and at least one not yet credited for the current day, calling the hourly setInterval's callback (accrueInterest(store) at src/server.js:163) runs synchronously on the Node event loop; any HTTP request already in flight or newly arriving during that window is delayed by the job's full runtime (empirically ~2.65s for 30k accounts, worse for more, growing super-linearly because each credited account triggers an O(n) store.update scan).

sites.title: Hourly job blocks event loop under load

confirmed.reasoning: Read src/server.js:161-165: the setInterval callback calls accrueInterest(store) synchronously inside the same process that runs http.createServer, with no worker thread, chunking, or yield point. Read src/interest.js:23-43: the for-loop walks every row from store.all('accounts') and, for each account not yet credited today, calls store.update (src/store.js:91-98), which does Array.findIndex — an O(n) scan — making the full first-run-of-the-day job O(n^2) in account count. Confirmed previously this only ran inside the separate one-shot scripts/run-jobs.mjs process (unaffected by server load) by reading that file and git history; this diff is the one that wires it into src/server.js, so it is correctly identified as introduced by this diff. I reproduced the complexity directly: a benchmark against accrueInterest with a store-like fake (O(n) findIndex update, matching the real store) gave 1000->28ms, 5000->78ms, 20000->816ms, 50000->5867ms, closely matching the finder's own numbers and showing clear super-linear growth. I then reproduced the blocking claim end-to-end using the real createServer + real Store with 30,000 accounts: a concurrent /health request fired just before calling accrueInterest(store) synchronously (exactly as the setInterval callback does) took 2674.7ms to resolve, matching the job's own 2654.7ms synchronous runtime almost exactly — i.e. the concurrent request was fully blocked for the job's duration. I also checked test/server.test.js and found no test exercising the setInterval wiring, confirming the regression is untested. I found no guard, batching, worker offload, or size cap anywhere in the diff or surrounding code that would prevent this.
confirmed.panel: 3 of 3 skeptics could not refute it

confirmed.title: Hourly timer races request handlers' store.save()
confirmed.rootCause: store.save() always writes to the same fixed per-process tmp path rather than a per-call-unique one, so the new hourly timer's store.save() call can race with a concurrent request handler's inline store.save() in the same process and collide on that shared tmp file.
confirmed.summary: store.save() writes to a fixed per-process tmp path, not a per-call-unique one; the new hourly timer calls it from the same process as every mutating route handler's inline save, and concurrent calls reliably collide.
confirmed.failure: Two store.save() calls overlapping in the same process (e.g. the hourly timer's save racing a concurrent request handler's inline save) share the literal tmp path `${file}.${pid}.tmp`; whichever rename() runs second gets ENOENT because the first already moved that shared tmp file to the real path. If the request handler's save loses, the client gets a false 500 for a mutation that already committed in memory, inviting a retry that creates a duplicate deposit/transfer (no idempotency key exists). If the timer's save loses, that hour's interest credit stays unpersisted and lastAccruedOn already marks the account as done for today, so it isn't retried until some other save happens to flush the whole store; a restart before that happens loses the credit.

sites.title: Hourly timer races request handlers' store.save()

confirmed.reasoning: Read src/store.js:68-73: save() builds tmp = `${this.file}.${process.pid}.tmp`, fixed per process, not per-call. Reproduced the race directly against the real Store class: two concurrent save() calls on the same store/file in-process collided (second rename() rejected with ENOENT) in 50/50 trials, matching the finder's own empirical claim. Confirmed every cited call site: src/server.js:84-91 (POST /transfers), 96-101 (POST /deposits), and the 500 catch-all at 143-148 all do `await store.save()` inline with no locking. Confirmed no idempotency protection exists on deposit()/transfer() (src/transfers.js), so a client retry after a spurious 500 would create a real duplicate. Confirmed the new hourly timer (src/server.js:162-165) calls accrueInterest(store) then a fire-and-forget store.save() from the same process/store with no coordination against in-flight request saves. The interest-credit-lost scenario also holds: accrueInterest mutates in-memory data (including lastAccruedOn) synchronously before the async save, so if that save loses the race, the credit sits unpersisted and won't be re-attempted that day (lastAccruedOn already matches today) — though it would still be persisted by the next successful save from any route, so loss is only truly permanent on a restart before any other save succeeds, which the finder already caveats correctly. I could not find any guard, mutex, or serialization preventing this anywhere in the code.

refuted.title: Old-schema writer silently wipes lastAccruedOn, causing double interest
refuted.rootCause: Store.update() rebuilds rows via pick(SCHEMA, ...) using each process's own in-memory SCHEMA, so a still-running old-code process (lacking lastAccruedOn in its SCHEMA) silently drops that field on any write during a rolling deploy, defeating the daily-credit guard — and the new 'safe to run twice' test only runs within one in-process store/schema, so it cannot detect this mixed-version data loss.
refuted.summary: Store.update() rebuilds a row via pick(SCHEMA, {...existing, ...patch}), so any account write made by a still-running old server (old SCHEMA, no lastAccruedOn) silently drops the new field, defeating the hourly job's 'already credited today' guard.
refuted.failure: docs/deploy.md:8 documents that two copies run against one file during a deploy. During that window: (1) the new server's hourly job credits an account and sets lastAccruedOn (src/interest.js:33-37); (2) the old, not-yet-upgraded server (whose SCHEMA at src/store.js:12, pre-PR, lacks lastAccruedOn) handles any unrelated account write for that account -- a deposit (src/transfers.js:47), a transfer (src/transfers.js:26-27), a close (src/accounts.js:50), or an interest-rate change (src/accounts.js:63) -- and Store.update's pick()-based full-row rebuild silently strips lastAccruedOn from the stored row, regardless of what the patch contains; (3) the new server's hourly job runs again later the same day, sees lastAccruedOn missing, and credits interest for that account a second time that day. I reproduced this end-to-end with the real pick/update logic from both the pre-PR and current SCHEMA: after an initial credit sets lastAccruedOn to '2026-03-02', one old-schema update (a routine deposit-style balanceCents write) removes the field, and a subsequent accrueInterest() call on the same day credits the account again (accounts: 1, cents: 14), instead of being skipped. This directly contradicts the PR's stated guarantee at src/interest.js:19-21 ('Safe to run as often as you like') and the README's removed 'not safe to run twice' caveat -- the feature is unsafe precisely during the rollout window the repo's own docs/deploy.md says is normal.

sites.title: Old-schema writer silently wipes lastAccruedOn, causing double interest
New test doesn't cover the rollout double-accrual scenario

refuted.why: The claim's own narrative says 'the new server's hourly job runs again later the same day, sees lastAccruedOn missing, and credits interest for that account a second time' -- i.e. the SAME new-code server process, after an old-code process wrote+saved an unrelated update. But src/server.js:159-163 opens the Store ONCE at startup (`const store = await Store.open(file)`) and the setInterval hourly job (src/server.js:162-166) calls accrueInterest on that SAME long-lived in-memory store object every tick; it never re-reads the file from disk between ticks. I built a reproduction with two real Store instances sharing one file: a 'new' process (current src/store.js, SCHEMA includes lastAccruedOn) and an 'old' process (a copy of store.js with lastAccruedOn removed from SCHEMA.accounts, modelling pre-PR code). Sequence: new process credits interest (lastAccruedOn='2026-03-02') and saves; old process performs an unrelated balance update on the same account using its own in-memory row (which never had lastAccruedOn) and saves, which does overwrite the on-disk file without the field, confirming pick()/update() behave as claimed for the write itself. But when the SAME new-process object's accrueInterest() is invoked again that same day (exactly as the claim's step 3 describes), the result is `{accounts: 0, cents: 0}` -- it correctly skips, because its own in-memory row still has lastAccruedOn set and is never affected by what the old process wrote to disk. Double-crediting only appears if a *fresh* new-code process is started and re-reads the clobbered file (a restart) -- a precondition the claim never states and that contradicts its own wording ('the new server's hourly job runs again', not 'a new new-server instance starts'). Separately, docs/deploy.md and the README's 'one process per ledger file' limitation already existed in the baseline commit (89da56f), before this diff, and the pick()/SCHEMA full-row-rebuild mechanism is unchanged by this PR -- the same hazard already applied identically to the currency and interestRateBps fields added by earlier migrations. So even granting a restart, this is a pre-existing architectural characteristic rather than something this diff introduces. The failure as described (same running new server re-crediting on its next tick) cannot occur; the only way to produce it requires an unstated process restart, making the claim's mechanism incorrect.

missed.what: accrueInterest only ever credits one fixed day's worth of interest per call, gated purely by `lastAccruedOn !== today` (src/interest.js:30). If the job fails to run at all during some calendar day — server down, mid-deploy, crash-looping, or simply restarted (which resets the hourly setInterval and needs a fresh, uninterrupted hour before its next tick) — that day's interest is silently and permanently lost for every account; the next successful run only ever adds one more day, never a catch-up for days that were skipped. The PR's own stated motivation is to stop depending on the operator's (more host-level, restart-independent) cron scheduler, which quietly trades that for a job whose correctness now depends on the Node process itself staying up continuously for at least one hour within every calendar day, with no persisted recovery for when it doesn't.
missed.why: correctness/data-integrity looked at whether a single run computes and credits correctly (and caught the local/UTC mismatch) but not at whether a run that never happens is ever recovered. background-job-robustness-in-server-process examined the job blocking or racing while it runs, not the consequence of it not running at all. migrations-and-rollout only checked that the new field is additive. None of those angles compares the job's new uptime-coupled trigger against the daily-accrual math's lack of catch-up logic — a cross-commit consequence, since the 'skip if already credited today' guard (new in this PR) and the 'always exactly one day per run' math (pre-existing) only become dangerous together.

missed.what: docs/deploy.md documents that 'two copies can run against one file during a deploy,' with rollout rules written entirely around migration additivity. This PR turns interest accrual from a short-lived, operator-invoked external script into a timer living inside every long-running server process (src/server.js:162). From now on, during every deploy's overlap window, both the old and new server copies independently run their own hourly accrueInterest + store.save() against the same file from their own in-memory snapshot — each capable of silently clobbering the other's concurrent writes (deposits, transfers, closures) via the last-writer-wins full-file rewrite in Store.save(), unconditionally on a timer rather than only in response to traffic.
missed.why: migrations-and-rollout (already run) verified only that the new `lastAccruedOn` field is additive-safe; it wasn't positioned to notice the same commit changes who else writes to the file during the overlap window the doc already describes. The scout's 'Hourly timer races request handlers' store.save()' finding is about one process's own event-loop interleaving, not about two separate OS processes each loading, mutating and overwriting the same file — a distinct, now much more frequent failure mode precisely because this PR embeds the job in every running copy instead of an external, deploy-independent invocation.

missed.what: README.md:10, left untouched by this diff, still reads `node scripts/run-jobs.mjs interest   # one day's interest; the scheduler runs it daily` — directly contradicting the bullet this same PR did update a few lines down ('The server runs it every hour; an account already credited today is skipped.') and the removed 'not safe to run twice' caveat. An operator reading only the Quick Start block will still believe they must configure a daily scheduler, the exact habit the PR's description says it exists to eliminate.
missed.why: No angle reviews prose for internal consistency across unrelated sections of a doc file the diff only partially edits; migrations-and-rollout and boundary-contract looked at schema/field-level contracts, not whether the README now contradicts itself. It's a behaviour the PR's own description promises ('the README's not-safe-to-run-twice limitation is gone') but the file itself only half-delivers.
